lesson.title: Manchester Encoding: A Clock Hidden Inside Every Bit
lesson.summary: Manchester encoding guarantees a signal transition in the middle of every single bit period, trading extra bandwidth for a built in clock that never lets a receiver drift out of sync.
lesson.body:
The general encoding chapter laid out the core problem with a naive scheme like NRZ: a receiver often recovers its clock from transitions in the incoming signal, so long runs of identical bits, which produce no transitions at all, let that recovered clock drift out of alignment. Manchester encoding solves this problem directly, by design, rather than as an accident of the data pattern. Every single bit period, whether the bit is a 1 or a 0, contains exactly one guaranteed transition right in the middle of that period. The direction of that transition, not the level before or after it, is what carries the bit's value.

One common convention, used in classic Ethernet (IEEE 802.3, as in 10BASE-T), encodes a 1 as a low to high transition in the middle of the bit period and a 0 as a high to low transition. You may encounter the opposite convention in other references; what matters is that the direction of the mid bit transition, not an absolute voltage level, is what carries the meaning. Because every bit forces its own mid bit transition regardless of what came before or after, a Manchester decoder always has a fresh edge to resynchronize against at least once per bit period, exactly the self clocking property the encoding chapter described as desirable.

Work through an example using that Ethernet convention to encode the bit sequence 1, 0, 1, 1, 0. A bit of 1 is low for the first half of its period and high for the second half; a bit of 0 is high for the first half and low for the second half. Laying out the ten half bit levels in order gives: low, high (bit 1) then high, low (bit 0) then low, high (bit 1) then low, high (bit 1) then high, low (bit 0). Notice what happens between the third and fourth bits, both of which are 1: the third bit ends high, but the fourth bit needs to start low, so an extra transition appears right at that bit boundary, on top of the mid bit transitions both bits already required. Everywhere else in this sequence, consecutive bits happen to end and begin at matching levels, so no extra boundary transition is needed there. This is the general pattern: Manchester encoding always has one transition per bit at the middle, plus an additional transition at a bit boundary whenever two consecutive bits share the same value.

That extra transition is also the cost of the scheme. Because a Manchester encoded signal can change twice within a single bit period in the worst case, it occupies roughly twice the bandwidth that a same bit rate NRZ signal would need on the same channel, a real engineering trade off between reliable clocking and spectral efficiency. This is exactly why classic 10 Mbps Ethernet used Manchester encoding, where the extra bandwidth was affordable, while later, much faster Ethernet standards moved to other line codes that pack more bits into less bandwidth and recover clocking through other means, since doubling the bandwidth requirement at gigabit speeds would be far more costly.
